articleTitle: Using Stage-Gate Processes effectively for managing technology-based projects
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. As a management tool, the Stage-Gate Process provides a template for planning, organizing and controlling of projects, especially useful for technology-based projects with complex work and organizational interfaces. Based on field studies of best-in-class practices, the paper discusses techniques for setting up the Stage-Gate Process properly as an integrated part of a modern project management system. The important role of cross-functional linkages, involvement, commitment, communications and decision making are emphasized. Recommendations for applying the Stage-Gate Process in an engineering project environment are made.

articleTitle: Kaizen at Morris Electronics: key to competitive success
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The paper describes the key aspects of the continuous improvement system at Morris Electronics Limited, an Indo-Japanese joint venture firm, that has contributed to dramatic improvements in productivity and sustained competitiveness. It also highlights the evolution of the collaboration between Morris and Hitachi Metals and its impact on the development of higher level competencies.

articleTitle: The Australian patent system
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given, as follows. Obtaining a patent is an important means of protecting the intellectual property of local as well as foreign individuals, companies and institutions in Australia. This paper provides an overview of the functions of the Australian Patent Office together with the legal infrastructure in Australia. A review on the procedures for obtaining patent protection in Australia is also provided.

articleTitle: Metrics from an SEI level 3 software process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This paper discusses measured results from a certified SEI level 3 process collected over three years and six internal software releases. Significant quality and productivity improvements were observed with consistent results attained even as the development team's size and membership varied. The subject software was developed for NASA/McDonnell Douglas and the space station program at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.

articleTitle: Intelligent concurrent engineering system for product development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. A framework for smart product modeling in a knowledge-based concurrent engineering environment is presented. The paper describes a case study that highlights developmental and implementation issues.

articleTitle: Business process engineering by design
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Design of manufacturing operations in a new enterprise, where only product design has existed before, requires effective communication. Using process flowcharts as foundational design elements allows business functions to be interconnected with a minimal amount of misunderstanding. This paper describes an approach for selecting systems, developing procedures and training programs, and establishing operational metrics.

articleTitle: Incremental reengineering
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Reengineering, introduced at the start of the 1990s, hit the industrial world with a bang! However, three negative elements surfaced fairly rapidly: implementation costs, high failure rates, and the more serious "downsizing" phenomenon, which often followed reengineering applications. "Incremental reengineering" is proposed which virtually eliminates all three negative elements.

articleTitle: Where Are We Headed With Technology Transfer?
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Development of MOT awareness in engineering and management courses in higher education
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Students on engineering and management courses need to be aware of the issues related to management of technology (MOT). This paper discusses how the depth and clarity of such an awareness may be facilitated by analyzing the impact of technology on management key roles identified at the academic levels at which such courses are offered.

articleTitle: Energy industry since NAFTY: an analysis of the winners and losers
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given, The energy industry, along with a few select others, is large enough and political enough to warrant a full chapter by itself in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). The role that each country has historically played cannot be overemphasized. The negotiations were delicate. Since the agreement, however, the growth numbers show that the industry has grown very well despite the peso collapse. This analysis shows which countries have won and which have lost through the negotiations and through the resulting trade relationships. A picture for the future is subsequently described.

articleTitle: New Software Technologies Streamline Product Design & Development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Relationship of technology and market in an innovation process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Technological innovation will play an important role in the future. The "S" curve describes an evolution of technology. During this period of dominance of R&D and the maturity of technology, critical times exist for strategic decisions. These strategic decisions include a variety of criteria and depend also on the capability to develop a market. The authors discuss the relationship between the technological "S" and market development as a tool for an optimization of product and market evolution as well as strategic policy. They present a case study as an example of that topic and discuss the suitable policy for small high-tech companies.

articleTitle: Management systems for processing of food industry waste
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. There are a lot of ideas on how to improve waste processing systems. Despite protracted efforts to improve operations, there has been little progress. This study provides a systems approach to the solution.

articleTitle: The mapping of corporate organizational values
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. This paper examines corporate values in terms of sets of related issues and the interaction of these sets with values held by individuals within organizations. A general methodology is proposed that allows corporate values to be mapped into both attitudes and management style required to implement and support organizational change.

articleTitle: Management Systems For Processing Of Food Industry Waste
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Designing a technology commercialization game plan for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has not traditionally been concerned with science and technology commercialization. In March 1997, NOAA launched the Center for Technology Innovation in Charleston, South Carolina, USA-a region not generally known for technology entrepreneurship. This paper discusses the antecedents to NOAA's launching this experiential learning laboratory and steps taken to make it successful.

articleTitle: The creation of agile people to facilitate collaboration
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The generalizable features of the best agile practices from a host of industries are presented. Examples from companies that were using precepts of agility to facilitate collaboration are highlighted along with the results of data collected from over 15 in-depth company studies of the people-side of agility. This research in this area is based upon a research project sponsored by the Agility Forum in Bethlehem, PA, USA.

articleTitle: The customer impact of software quality
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Most software companies recognize the need for understanding their customers' feature requirements; however, fewer understand their customers' quality requirements. This paper describes the customers of today's software, gives examples of how they might be impacted by different aspects of product quality, and describes how software companies may in turn be impacted.

articleTitle: Strategy for knowledge development in long term system's re-engineering processes
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. The Canadian government is presently investing about half a billion dollars in the reengineering and retooling of its income security programs on a national basis. The author was brought in to develop and implement a partnering strategy for both private and public sector business partners involved. The presentation focuses on the strategy and its implementation process.

articleTitle: Information Management Of Integrated Design
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: A SW assisted Baldrige based self-assessment process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary for only given as follows. Discussion of the approach, deployment and results of the use of a SW assisted MBNQA criteria based self-assessment process. A service/support operating business element of a major international company was the pilot project. The initial results indicated opportunities for improvement. Re-assessment is scheduled for September 1996 and changes will be used for future direction.

articleTitle: Conceptual modeling for distributed information system development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Distributed software development has become more and more important. In this paper, a powerful conceptual framework for such distributed development has been presented using a knowledge representation language, Telos, by concentration on the semantics of their domains. This framework is developed and based on careful analysis and abstraction of a real world case. By creating rich ontology, this paper provides knowledge level analysis for future distributed software development.

articleTitle: Multi-institutional Collaborative R&D Environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Polo International and global software marketing
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Polo International and SOFTEX 2000 in Brazil have established international technology assessment and marketing linkages in Europe, Asia, and the USA. Polo International was admitted into the Austin Technology Incubator in 1995. This paper discusses the challenges and opportunities faced by this relatively small software company in meeting its objective of establishing a global marketing strategy.

articleTitle: Managing an internal service organization in a large corporation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Large corporations need various internal service functions. However, these are generally considered to be overhead and are subject to considerable scrutiny. A high level of service and customer satisfaction are important. Service performance needs to be measured. The organization needs to be viewed as a service function rather than a regulatory function. Internal service organizations should also consider possible roles for managing contracted services. A business as usual attitude is not the way to manage an internal service organization in today's corporate environment.

articleTitle: Technology roadmapping: the integration of strategic and technology planning for competitiveness
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Technology planning is becoming critical with the rapid development and obsolescence of technologies. Technology roadmapping provides a tool for selecting which technologies to pursue in what timeframes. This paper provides a framework for technology roadmaps, describes the roadmapping process, and reviews its application.

articleTitle: Assembly planning in a virtual environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper presents novel tools to assist manual assembly in an virtual environment. While assembling virtual components, the user's actions are logged and an assembly plan is produced. Prototyping is reduced and concurrency is enhanced using such tools. Successful pilot studies have now been completed.

articleTitle: Supplier involvement in new product development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This paper focuses on the increasingly important role of suppliers in new product development (NPD) programs of American companies. Limited attention has been paid to the contributions that suppliers can make to the effectiveness and efficiency of the NPD process. The comments made are intended to apply to the case of an original equipment supplier providing a component to a customer who is also the final manufacturer and marketer of a new product.

articleTitle: Industrial concerns in technology selection
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Technology selection is very important in all technology-based companies. Most methodologies that have been developed to assist and improve this process have not been widely used. This paper uses the findings of a study to identify a set of design criteria for a practical and useful methodology.

articleTitle: Innovation forecasting
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Technological forecasting is premised on a certain orderliness of the innovation process. Myriad studies of technological substitution, diffusion and transfer processes have yielded conceptual models of what matters for successful innovation. Yet most technological forecasts key on limited empirical measures quite divorced from those innovation process models. The authors glean a number of concepts from various innovation models, then present an array of bibliometric measures that offer promise of operationalizing these concepts. Judicious combination of such bibliometrics with other forms of evidence offers an enriched form of technological forecasting that they name "innovation forecasting". This provides a good means to combine technological trends, mapping of technological interdependencies and competitive intelligence to produce a viable forecast. They illustrate this approach by assessing the prospects for ceramic engine technologies.

articleTitle: Success factors of project management: the critical few-an empirical investigation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: During recent years, project management has been firmly established as a concept for organizing extraordinary, innovative as well as strategic endeavors. However, still many of these projects fail. What are the recommendations that research can provide to practising managers? This paper aims to provide general recommendations regarding project management. This effort is based on the assumption that the project success depends on a relatively small number of variables-the so-called success factors.

articleTitle: Knowledge discovery and sharing in an information system
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The collection, organization, retrieval and interpretation of knowledge and information are not only important to an organization's success but vital to its survival. This paper deals with the knowledge conversion within/between tacit knowledge and explicit knowledge in new product development. Based on the framework of NII services, an Internet service for knowledge discovery and sharing, is proposed in the context of their on-going development of an information system for knowledge amplification.

articleTitle: The evolutionary process of secondary innovation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. In contrast with "first innovation" which generates and dominates the technological paradigms, and is usually carried out in developed countries, this paper explores the evolutionary process of "secondary innovation" which is performed on the basis of acquired technologies, particularly in developing countries (DCs). By presenting a general conceptual technology source-centered model of secondary innovation with four sequential sub-models: imitation; assimilation; exploitation; and exploration, as a framework, this paper studies the evolutionary processes of secondary innovation as in one technological cycle (within a defined technological paradigm) and the linear and nonlinear dynamics of secondary innovation in DCs. The key issues to appropriate "late-comer's advantages" are also explored.

articleTitle: A reverse logistics supply chain model within a remanufacturing environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. A recoverable product environment is one in which all, or as much as feasible, of the product is recovered and put back in use after the initial product life is over, rather than discarding the used product. Integral to the recoverable product environment is the recoverable manufacturing system which focuses on recovering the product and extending its life through remanufacture or repair. The flow of materials and products in this environment occurs both from the customer to the remanufacturer, and from the remanufacturer to the customer. Since most of the products and materials are conserved, this essentially forms a closed-loop logistics system. Acquisition of the used product from the consumer base, remanufacturing it at specified locations, and distributing it back to the consumer base are important activities which must be carefully coordinated if a remanufacturing firm is to remain profitable. We provide a mixed integer programming model to accomplish the coordination. The model seeks to minimize the total cost of this process. The model is solved using data generated on the basis of a real remanufacturing facility using the GAMS modeling package. The solution provides the location of the manufacturing/distribution facilities, the product types collected at each facility for remanufacturing from various collection zones, and the distribution of the remanufactured products to the various customer zones, so as to minimize the costs of distribution, inventory and remanufacturing.

articleTitle: Tqm In Maintenance To Improve Manufacturing Performance
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Technological benchmarking of products using the data envelopment analysis: an application to segments 'A' and 'B' of the Italian car market
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper uses data envelopment analysis (DEA) to carry out a competitive benchmarking study to compare 29 car models of the Italian market segments 'A' and 'B' sold in the last twenty years. Product features are identified and some indexes are constructed to implement DEA.

articleTitle: Integrated configuration management system (ICMS) for computer system development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Configuration management is defined as the activities identifying the configuration items, which are the outputs throughout the entire development life cycle, controlling the changes to the configuration, and managing the information related configuration management activities. Hardware and software components in a computer system are hierarchically and functionally related with each other. Such complexity prevents the researchers and the developers from building an efficient configuration management system that fits into a computer system development project. This paper describes a simple and integrated configuration management system methodology, which can be applied to the development environment for large or midrange computer systems.

articleTitle: An effective structure for Technology Computer-Aided Design organization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This paper describes the merits and demerits of presently organized Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD) Structures and proposes an effective structure of TCAD organization for the continued success of today's semiconductor design and manufacturing companies. This study shows that the different TCAD functions are either distributed among the primary groups in the value chain of the firm or organized under a primary corporate function. Each distributed function of TCAD focuses on application specific usage to assist the respective primary function. On the other hand, an integrated TCAD group provides software and hardware support, application and user training, benchmarking of tools, and out-sourcing coordination. Traditionally, the semiconductor companies rely on outside expertise and support for critical usage of TCAD for their immediate needs and maintain a cost-effective structure for TCAD. However, the lack of in-house expertise and corporate support to address the critical issues of TCAD may cost competitive advantage of the firm in the long run. In general, the success of advanced product design, technology development, and manufacturing relies on efficient TCAD application methodologies, accurate process and device models, efficient algorithms for higher simulation throughput, and skilled engineering staff. In addition, to realize the full potential of TCAD in today's integrated circuit design and manufacturing, proper integration of TCAD tools into a system is extremely important.

articleTitle: Remanufacturing
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Deterioration of our ecosystem has forced government, consumers and manufacturers to question production methods, products used, and product disposal. It is becoming no longer feasible to make goods without taking into consideration the end of a product's useful life. Remanufacturing as the ultimate form of recycling is a relatively unknown end-of-life process which demands further development. The product life cycle and its impact on the environment are discussed in this paper.

articleTitle: The role of culture in information technology diffusion in organizations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Internal factors that influence information technology adoption in organizations include organizational size, centralization, formalization, and organizational culture. Organizational culture can play a crucial role in the investment or adoption of information technology and the subsequent diffusion of technology within the organization. This paper investigates the role of organizational culture in information technology diffusion.

articleTitle: Factors affecting information technology transfer and innovation diffusion in health care
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The transfer of electronic mail as a new technology was examined in over 60 academic health centers in the USA by surveying 1,335 individuals. Innovation attributes are important predictors for both the spread of usage (internal diffusion) and depth of usage (infusion) of electronic mail. In addition, organizational and boundary-spanning attributes are significant predictors for diffusion. Ease of use, visibility, communication, champions and generation of marketing intelligence were significant individual variables.

articleTitle: Structural comparison of data envelopment analysis and multiple objective linear programming [management performance studies]
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The concept of efficiency plays an important role both in data envelopment analysis (DEA) and multiple objective linear programming (MOLP). Despite this and other apparent similarities, DEA and MOLP research have developed separately. Structurally, the DEA formulation to identify efficient units is quite similar to the MOLP model based on the reference point approach.

articleTitle: Organizational and managerial correlates of radical technological innovation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Interview data from eight radical technological innovation projects suggest the following factors as contributing to project success: strong support of committed champions; individual characteristics of those champions; accessibility and support by top management; and significant or serendipitous events. Factors acting to suppress technical project progress were: corporate culture; and current requirements on operating units.

articleTitle: Towards the development of an Integrated Building Management System
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. We define an Integrated Building Management System as a complex, multi-level, multi-objective, integrated, interrelated and complete intelligent design management information system capable of assisting building design process from the inception phase through management and maintenance phases. The proposed system will combine all different activities during the building and construction design activity. Arguably introducing such a system requires up to a certain degree a change in the working conditions and strategies. While it is true that the introduction of automation into these processes will affect from the one hand the working protocols of building designers and managers; on the other hand these automation processes should also be based on the way in which building design is carried out in the real world. The changes of conditions and possibilities of the building design and management working environments will result from the combination of the two. This paper suggests prerequisites for the realisation and the management of integrated building design environments. It addresses the crucial issues related to the recognition, definition and implementation of advanced technologies in building engineering design with an emphasis on information control and the management of planning process.

articleTitle: Using the value chain model as a method of prioritizing green reengineering efforts
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: During the last century, humankind has advanced at an incredible rate, and, while many are focusing on profits and efficiency, the natural environment has suffered. The senior management of many companies have begun to take an interest in reducing the impact to the environment and have begun changing their business processes. While reassessing operations makes sense, finding a starting place has been difficult. We propose a new method of prioritizing process changes using a synthesis of business process reengineering, TQM, and value chain analysis. We call this framework green reengineering.

articleTitle: The management of intelligence-assisted finite element analysis technology
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches to finite element analysis (FEA), have had tentative degrees of success over the last few years and some authors have argued that effective FEA can help in the manufacture, reliability and safety aspects of engineered artefacts. The author of this paper reviews how such AI techniques have been applied and in this light, the author then uses a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM), to develop a framework for the management of intelligence-assisted FEA.

articleTitle: Impact of technology on employment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Employment in any industry is impacted by the introduction of new technology whose objective is to increase productivity. The initial result of such technological introduction is the reduction of workers to some extent. At some point, the productivity from the new technology reaches a plateau. If the business requirements are increasing, it is possible that the firm or industry must start to hire new workers to meet the increased industry demands. The introduction of technological improvements starts the cycle anew. This paper presents a model and empirical data, which illustrates these employment cycles. The data presented in this paper is for several Turkish industries. The analytical model could apply to most industries, but additional empirical data will be needed to very this assertion.

articleTitle: Managing technological innovation portfolio: experiences and lessons in China
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Over the past decade, although people have attached much attention to the innovative activities in firms, executives often view the innovation process as a static, linear process, and often limit their strategic consideration on technology innovation in an isolated and separated way. The innovation process is actually a dynamic, nonlinear and systematic process, which makes traditional innovation management too simple and inappropriate for use in a long-term view. By reviewing these works and the investigation results of some leading firms in China, this paper advances a new paradigm for innovation management-portfolio innovation-which can be used to integrate technological, organizational and institutional factors from a strategic and systematic view.

articleTitle: Strategic project management: from ad-hocracy to standardization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The author argues that project managers should get off the ad-hoc approach that ends up with daily fire fighting and keeps them from seeing the project's big picture. Rather, they should concentrate on capturing the returns that standardized project management holds. This paper shows how to visualize standardized project management, and having visualized it, create it.

articleTitle: TQM in maintenance to improve manufacturing performance
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper provides a case study of implementing total quality management (TQM) into a maintenance function within a traditional manufacturing company. It identifies the key quality related activities taken by the maintenance management team within the company and shows that the results of implementing TQM into maintenance can be quite dramatic in contributing to improved manufacturing performance.

articleTitle: Intelligent decision support system for equipment diagnosis and maintenance management
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This paper reports the research project which has been carried out at the Central Textiles (HK) Ltd. in Hong Kong. The main objective of the project is to help the company to approach an integrated maintenance management system by using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This AI-based maintenance management system schedules and controls maintenance activities under considerations of not only the working conditions of equipment in the company but also the production quality, production system efficiency and production cost.

articleTitle: Intermediate performance measures in engineering projects
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Conventional methods for measuring progress during an engineering project include the use of supervisors and milestones, and a variety of scheduling and cost procedures. This exploratory survey draws upon the literature and inputs from engineering managers to identify other measures employed to provide a comparison of planned with actual progress.

articleTitle: Higher order technological learning, strategic assets, core capabilities, and market performance in technology-driven firms: an empirical study
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This study explores the link between higher and lower order technological learning processes and firm market performance (profitability) via firm strategic assets creation and core capabilities deployment. The model used is one where technological learning facilitates technology transfer which enhances the firms strategic assets and core capabilities thus potentially increasing firm profitability. The theoretical concepts of higher and lower order technological learning are established, its dual nature as technical and administrative learning is defined, and its role in strategic assets and core capabilities development is examined. Technological learning is the medium or "tool" for facilitating and managing technology transfer and is defined as the process by which a technology-driven firm creates, renews, and upgrades its latent and enacted capabilities based on its stock of explicit and tacit resources. Qualitative findings on technological learning are correlated to the quantitative evidence, namely firm profitability data that cover the time period examined (1970-95). The quantitative analysis is based on correlation and therefore evidence of relationships between the levels of learning and profitability as well as between the levels of learning and changes in profitability due to a learning effect. The hypotheses testing based on our empirical data indicates that the levels of learning do not have any significant correlation to profitability. The paper attempts to define further research on the topic as well as reasons to explain these phenomena.

articleTitle: Internationalization of R&D and global management of technological competencies within transnational corporations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The internationalization of research and innovation raised serious coordination problems for multinational corporations. These companies respond by concentrating technological competencies at specific locations. This paper analyses new location factors driving the globalization of research and innovation and presents criteria for the establishment of competence centers.

articleTitle: The role of client/server computing technology in the management of global enterprises
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Client/server technology is a revolution that is forever altering how we build and manage information processing systems. Client/server is a realization of a new kind of increasingly distributed information networks accessible from anywhere at any-time. The rapid growth of client/server technology is due to powerful technical and economic forces. Several technical trends are converging around client/server technology. These include faster, smaller and standardized computer components, improved distributed communications and increased information dissemination. Strong economic forces include emphasis on operational effectiveness, demand for market driven quality, need to increase enterprise responsiveness, and reengineering of business processes and information flows. These advantages make client/server technology very attractive for organizations facing pressures of increased global competition. This paper defines client/server computing and summarizes some of the technical and business-related forces making this technology popular. This paper also explores how client/server technology is used to create and manage information-driven enterprises and maximize user productivity.

articleTitle: A spreadsheet implementation of QFD and systems engineering approaches to support concurrent engineering
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: For an organisation to sustain its competitive advantage, there is a strong need for timely adjustment to ever rapidly changing customer demands. To achieve this goal, known customer needs must be prioritised and transformed into organised downstream design requirements. This paper describes how a spreadsheet framework has been developed which incorporates a modified quality function deployment (QFD) and systems engineering process (SEP) for product development and planning. The application of the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) is used as a means of ranking top level user requirements. The methodology provides a pro-active means and a strong link between quantified user requirements that are prioritised and product design/performance by assuring that down-stream design incorporated into trade-off decisions. An example is also presented to test and evaluate the spreadsheet approach in heavy engineering projects.

articleTitle: Methods for improving the quality of new product innovations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Continually producing high-quality products is critical to competitive advantage. We studied 75 new product development projects in ten large firms to test potential strategic and process antecedents. Seven factors were found to significantly increase product quality: perceived importance, rewards, project stream, internal sourcing, overlap, turfguarding, and milestones. Implications are discussed.

articleTitle: Patterns of knowledge generating networks
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The paper presents a concept of knowledge generating network as a model of an R&D system. Conceptual, personal and organizational networks are reviewed and an integrated model of a knowledge generating system for technological innovation is proposed. This model assumes that organizational networks support connections among individual researchers (personal network) who create new concepts and solutions which add to the conceptual network. A hypothesis is presented concerning possibility of using the neural network as a metaphor in further studies on R&D networks.

articleTitle: New technologies and industrial automation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper presents a critical review of the impact of new technologies on industrial automation from a systems engineering point of view. The discussion covers some of the important technical and organizational issues encountered in the design of flexible automation systems, and provides an overview of the new trends in modelling and control. It is recommended that any industrial automation project needs to be formulated and implemented within the context of cognitive systems engineering.

articleTitle: Metaphorical focusing devices for novel product conceptualization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The authors explore, how metaphorical reasoning may stimulate the diversity and number of alternatives that managers can conceive of when struggling with technological and market uncertainty, i.e. during new product conceptualization. Metaphorical reasoning may break up decision makers' inadequate cognitive technological maps in the face of emerging markets and technologies.

articleTitle: QuickView: an assessment tool for small- to medium-sized manufacturing firms
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Government-sponsored manufacturing extension services, modeled after cooperative extension, have been established to provide technical and business assistance to small to medium sized manufacturers (SME). Assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of SME has become a necessary diagnostic procedure for manufacturing extension services. One such assessment procedure, QuickView, has clearly demonstrated superior results as a preliminary diagnostic tool.

articleTitle: Toward a fundamental differentiation between projects
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The authors contend that it is possible to look beyond immediate project shortcomings for some pivotal dimensions that would enable better correlation between different types of project and appropriate styles of management. The authors suggest that all projects, or at least their major elements, can be typified according to the fundamental differences in the type of product produced and the type of work required to produce that product. Two fundamentally different types of product are identified as 'tangible' and 'intangible' and similarly two types of work (effort) are identified as 'craft' and 'intellect'. These two dimensions together form a simple 2/spl times/2 matrix in which four fundamentally different types of project element can be found. These are represented by tangible-intellect, intangible-intellect, intangible-craft, and tangible-craft. The paper describes each of these four elements, their typical characteristics and example projects. Intuitively, one suspects that people involved in craft work respond better to being told what to do, while those involved in intellectual work expect to be allowed to think for themselves. These represent the need for very different styles of project management. In the course of the project life cycle, other project management styles are also no doubt required.

articleTitle: Managing engineering and technology means managing intellectual capital
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This paper describes a method for predictive management of engineering and technology via intellectual capital. It discusses the components of intellectual capital: market assets, intellectual property assets, human centred assets and infrastructure assets, and the role they play in the management of technology and engineering projects. A method for developing the "Dream Ticket" is explained as a means for focussing on critical success factors. The concept of the knowledgeable engineering organisation is introduced, and we contemplate whether engineering organisations know what they know. The structure of the organisational star is presented as a mechanism of identifying, documenting monitoring and growing competences, know-how, education and expertise from the perspective of the individual, and how it can be used as the basis for building a corporate know-how base. The corporate know-how base, an Intranet based system, is described as "open" within the organisation. It's function being to assist managers in putting engineering teams together, tracking the location of know-how, competence and experience within the organisation. Motivational factors to keep the organisational star up to date are discussed, and a mentoring system is proposed to validate, grow, and monitor competences from the perspective of the individual. Finally the paper concludes with the factors that the role of the engineering manager should include.

articleTitle: Cost-benefit analysis of ecological, technogenic and sociogenic security of society
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. The general purpose is control of risk of ecological, technogenic and sociogenic accidents. This concept is fixed on the basis of created software based on mathematical modeling. The obtained results are the characteristics of levels of recreative possibilities, intensity of regulatory gears and reserve of ecological system; the various scripts of liquidation of consequences of accidents; valuation of risk of occurrence of irreversible changes at different levels of organization of ecological system, prognosis of ecological situation.

articleTitle: Survey on tacit knowledge use in the R&D of Japanese companies
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Focusing on the use of tacit knowledge, the authors analyze the nature of intellectual activities in the R&D processes of the seven largest electronics companies in Japan using data obtained from a survey. The seven largest Japanese companies are Hitachi, Toshiba, NEC, Mitsubishi, Fujitsu, Matsushita and Sony.

articleTitle: Optimal sequential and parallel prototyping policies
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. When designing a new product or service, its developers must balance the expected profit of improving the design against the costs and time requirements of doing so. The authors propose to quantify this trade-off by modeling a latter stage of development, prototyping, as a search process. The decision makers choose how many prototypes to build, then observe the projected profit of each. Multiple parallel prototypes are modeled as n random draws from a continuous probability distribution. The model balances the cost of building and testing the parallel prototypes against improvements in expected profits. The authors also study the option to abandon the project when even the best prototype generates losses. Further, they investigate prototyping decisions for products consisting of independent components that must be compatible in order for the total system to be profitable. Process design also considers alternatives for improving particular process steps, but is complicated by the need for compatibility between these improved process steps.

articleTitle: Technology transfer models: an understandable but useless abstraction of reality?
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. In the first part of the paper, a brief overview of models and their use in technology management research is given. It is argued that models are useful tools to formalise problems and test hypothesis, and also to create common standards of communication or understanding. A simple taxonomy of models is proposed. It is suggested that models can be either dynamic or static, and either soft or hard. Dynamic models are generally predictive, whilst static models are generally descriptive. The rigour used in the model building process is described by the soft or hard nature of the model. Example of models falling under each category are given, and the type of models used in technology management research is examined. Most of those fall under the 'soft' models category. A number of technology transfer models are examined. As an example, the usefulness of a model of the technology transfer processes between university and small and medium sized enterprises is then considered, and it is suggested that an understanding of the processes involved can be achieved from various types of models, but that the frame of reference in which the model is built and read is an important factor to take into account when creating and using technology transfer models. Furthermore, the assumptions buried in different forms of representation may be a barrier to the usability between different sets of groups.

articleTitle: How you can develop a Skunk Works for your organization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Lockheed Martin received a contract to develop an experimental reusable rocket ship. The proposal emanated from its Skunk Works which successfully developed fourteen innovative products in record time. The methods developed to establish such a record are discussed in this paper.

articleTitle: New product technology-who makes the strategic decisions?
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This research examines data collected from chief executive officers (CEOs) and chief technology officers (CTOs) of Fortune "500" companies as to how new technology is acquired, and who plays a major role in the decisions. It is found that firms make use of chief technology officers and Scientific Advisory Committees in assisting in the difficult task of selecting appropriate new technology. The study in general indicates a greater participation of CEOs in the new product technology process, either personally or with and/or through the use of a CTO as part of their staff.

articleTitle: Reference models as a strategic issue for the construction of flexible production planning and control systems
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Today's production planning and control (PPC) systems often manifest a lack of adaptation to new processes. One way to build more flexible PPC systems consists in a first step of modeling the manufacturing processes and in a second one of executing the model as a PPC system. Furthermore, the authors have developed a method for the construction of PPC systems based on reference models.

articleTitle: Technology intelligence identifying and evaluating new technologies
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Technological change affects all business sectors, presenting threats as well as opportunities. Strategic planning requires technology intelligence to identify technological developments in time. A model linking market needs via innovation fields to the technological environment is proposed. We distinguish between technology fields based on technologies in use at the company and interesting technology fields which can be limited by future product functions and weak signals on technological trends. Based on this model a technology intelligence process consisting of formulation of information needs, selection of information sources, data collection and evaluation of information is described.

articleTitle: Rapid application development: major issues and lessons learned
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. It has often been noted that rapid application development (RAD) methodologies have revolutionized the software industry. However, do RAD tools/techniques really reduce product development time? How does RAD affect product quality? This paper explores some of these important issues based on in-depth interviews with practising software development managers.

articleTitle: Management of R&D in relation to corporate governance
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The main intention of management is to ensure the continued existence of the company. It is therefore necessary for a company to "live the present" and "pioneer the future". The latter administrative behaviour is referred to as "pioneering governance". The authors discuss R&D activities from the governance viewpoint.

articleTitle: Technology management with mathematical diffusion models
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The life time of each technology consists of phases following each other. The phases can be identified by the typical features driving the improvements in a phase. Theoretical and empirical studies on technology management cover a wide variety of different efforts to model these dynamics. The dynamics include features common to all technologies but also features individual to a certain technology only. This paper gives an overview of mathematical models diffusion dynamics. The aim of the paper is to increase understanding of the life cycle analysis of different technologies. Deeper understanding supports better quality of technology management from the managers point of view and increases the predictability of future changes as well as the engineering process in general.

articleTitle: Implementation of an integrated product development process for systems
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: A product development process reengineering was performed to improve competitive position and establish a consistent development process, based on best practices, across multiple divisions. The development process framework consists of cross-functional executive management teams, product development teams, a structured development process, and stage-gated decision checkpoint reviews. The implementation approach shown to be successful included diagnosis of current development process problems, formation of a cross-functional process customization team to perform the actual process design, creation of reviewer networks, pilot project implementation, and use of outside consultants. Crucial for deployment of the new development process were sustaining senior executives support, and making complementary organizational changes.

articleTitle: A "corporate technology stock" model-determining total R&D expenditure and effective investment pattern
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: A "corporate technology stock" model based on the concept of "depreciation" facilitates understanding of the corporate technological process and derives a numerical model and a formula for deciding R&D expenditure and high performance investment patterns. Numerical simulations revealed that the model accords satisfactorily with experience In industry, and provides a new methodology for the corporate management of technology.

articleTitle: Virtual team members: a case study in management of multiple projects in a limited resource environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This case study explores the use of virtual team members utilizing optimized communications to manage a greater number of projects without defocusing individual staff members from their primary project responsibilities. Staff members develop and maintain online guidelines and templates based on their strengths and experience. Project teams document and maintain project status, issues and questions online. Projects that require the expertise of staff members who have a different primary project utilize these staff members as virtual project team members. Virtual team members allocate a portion of their time viewing secondary projects online to review status, answer questions and make recommendations. Thus more project teams can operate simultaneously and efficiently.

articleTitle: Financing technological entrepreneurship: the role of strategic alliances in procuring early-stage seed capital
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: A significant gap exists in early-stage seed capital for technology-based new ventures. This article reports the results of a survey of embryonic firms in the southwestern United States, which received significant amounts of their initial capital from strategic partners. High levels of satisfaction with the alliance were reported by the capital recipients and the alliances tended to evolve into long-term relationships. The alliances were set up to gain access to risk capital as well as complementary tangible and intangible assets such as embodied technologies, patents, know-how, and distribution networks.

articleTitle: Project success: a multidimensional, strategic concept
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. What does project success mean? When a project is completed on time and within the original budget, is it a success? Or even when it fails to meet these objectives but succeeds in meeting its specified requirements, is it then a successfully completed project? The objective of this work is to develop a universal framework for the assessment of project success to help organizations cope with the above questions. We view project success as a strategic multidimensional concept where project efforts must be aligned with the strategic long-term goals of the organization. We employ in this study a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, and two data sets which included more than 140 projects. Using a project specific approach, our analysis resulted in four distinct success dimensions: (1) project efficiency, (2) impact on the customer, (3) direct business and organizational success, and (4) preparing for the future. These dimensions represent different points of view, different concerns of the organization, and different time horizons. We demonstrate how the relative importance of these dimensions varies with the time passed since project completion, as well as with the project type. Finally, we provide a set of guidelines for project managers and policy makers at the top level.

articleTitle: Exit interviews of technical personnel: missed opportunities, lost knowledge
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. In times of momentous turmoil and competition, organizations are constantly seeking more and better information to assist in improving their competitive position. An organization would be foolish to ignore the competitive environment. Likewise, an organization would be short sighted to disregard the knowledge possessed by its employees. Unfortunately, too many organizations fail to recognize the wealth of potentially useful information possessed by the employees who are departing the organization; whether a voluntary departure or involuntary termination, employees leaving an organization offer a largely untapped resource for collecting impressions of, experiences with, and knowledge about an organization and its activities. Only rarely is an attempt made to capture this knowledge or assess the underlying message that this knowledge may provide. This paper suggests that the use of exit interviews and/or exit surveys (EIS) would be a fruitful tool for capturing additional information that might be useful to the organization in developing short- and long-term strategic planning goals and as a diagnostic tool in identifying targets of change. An overview of the EIS literature is presented.

articleTitle: Fuzzy nonradial DEA measures of technical efficiency
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: When measuring technical efficiency, the notion of a radial distance measure may be replaced with the concept of a nonradial distance measure. Also, the assumption of crisp production plans may be substituted with the weaker assumption of fuzzy production plans. This paper merges these concepts and evaluates the efficiency performance of a newspaper preprint insertion production line.

articleTitle: Investment in learning capital: enhancing the rate of learning by doing in semiconductor manufacturing
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Learning by doing occurs in the semiconductor industry through manufacturing yield improvements that result in cost reductions. While all semiconductor firms learn through engineering analysis of production volume to improve yields, firms differ substantially in the level and rate of improvement of yields. In this paper, a set of physical and human capital factors is identified that influences the rate of learning by doing.

articleTitle: R&D organizational processes on suspension system for automobiles: a comparative analysis based on patents and academic publications
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The authors have developed a methodology that represents the dynamics of R&D organizations based on intellectual products such as patents and academic publications. The methodology has the advantages of objective procedures and the usage of data which are open to the public. This paper aims to analyze the characteristics of R&D organizational processes of companies in Japan and in the United States by using the methodology, and to compare them. It reveals the differences in interrelations in R&D organizations.

articleTitle: Methods and tools for first five steps of benchmarking process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Many enterprises confront serious difficulties when they decide to undertake a continuous improvement of their performance. Among the approaches which may help an enterprise to improve its performance, benchmarking is required today as one of the most efficient and effective management tools. However, benchmarking seems often lacking a modeled and theoretical thinking which hinders the benefits and makes difficult the reuse of realized experiments. The aim of this paper is to formalize the benchmarking process and to propose the tools and methods accompanying the steps of that process. The authors actual work focuses on the first two phases of the benchmarking process: measurement and self-analysis (phase 1); and determination of subject and partners of a benchmarking study (phase 2). For this purpose, related to the first phase, a method of diagnosis which is based on organizational modeling is employed. This method is based essentially on the assessment of internal customer satisfaction. In the second phase, three different data analysis methods are utilized. These methods are lexical analysis, and principal components and common factor analysis which are two multivariate analysis methods. These two phases serve the purpose of an internal benchmarking (comparison between different domains of activities in the enterprise) and of an external benchmarking (comparison between different enterprises). Three enterprises are selected for the benchmarking application. Related data are collected and analyzed, and results are reported.

articleTitle: Improving IT education in Estonian universities
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: After getting independence in 1992, Estonia started to develop its university system from the Soviet model towards the West European model. The restructuring of higher education is not easy; there is a lack of highly educated people. The reasons for that are manifold: after opening the borders, some highly skilled specialists moved abroad; industry and fast growing economy is competing with universities providing higher salaries to specialists; and in general, university work is not ranked on a high level in social status. The fast growing economy demands new kinds of skills traditionally not included in university education. Especially in the area of information technology, the problem is significant; the IT industry is growing fast and demands a growing amount of skilled people. To satisfy this demand, universities have implemented a development programme in co-operation with a network of some European universities. The development programme has four goals: (1) improvements in technical infrastructure; (2) dramatic growth in the amount of postgraduate students to satisfy the demand for university teachers; (3) improving the IT curricula to satisfy the changing needs of the industry and economy; and (4) development of university/industry co-operation. This paper describes these development activities, concentrating especially on the co-operation network of universities and the knowledge transfer from other countries, especially from Finland, to Estonia.

articleTitle: The Irish software industry. Lessons learned
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper details the origins and development of the Irish software industry, treating it as an example of successful technology management by a small developing country. From a situation with little or no industry, and no tradition in high technology sectors, Ireland has become one of the key centers for world software production.

articleTitle: Management of technical innovation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Based on over 200 studies in industry, government and research settings, the paper offers a preliminary contingency framework for technology managers to deploy the individual cognitive abilities of Remote Association and Differentiation in accordance with the tasks and phases of the innovation process.

articleTitle: Engineering and technology management education
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The educational component of engineering and technology management is continuing to grow at an impressive pace. The history of such programs goes back to early 1900s but the primary growth has been taking place since mid 1970s. There were less than 30 degree granting programs, worldwide, in 1976. That number has grown 6-fold in 20 years. As a result of these forces, the field has been showing a very strong growth pattern since mid-1970s. The earlier growth was in the United States, but in the last ten years, other countries have started to develop degree programs just as rapidly as the US. Close to 200 universities are now offering degrees in engineering and technology management, worldwide. Most of this growth is at the graduate level, with majority of the institutions offering Masters degrees, and an increasing number of them developing Ph.D. programs. This paper summarizes the results of a study conducted two years ago. It is the fifth such effort in a longitudinal study being conducted since 1976. More than 3,000 people were contacted in academic institutions throughout the world. Detailed information was obtained about the educational characteristics and research directions of the field. The findings are reported in the paper.

articleTitle: An innovative application of CSCW for solving engineering design problems
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Groupware is increasingly being used by engineering design teams to reach consensus on a range of issues relating to the design process. In this paper, the authors discuss the development and evaluation of a computer-supported collaborative work (CSCW) system in enhancing the effectiveness of cross-functional teams involved in the selection of the best layout for cellular manufacturing teams. The results are very promising for engineering design teams who are required to collaborate but are distributed in several locations.

articleTitle: Challenges of technology transfer from a Canadian National Research Facility
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper describes the challenges, importance and opportunities of transferring technology from accelerator laboratories. A few guidelines to achieve total quality management are discussed. The concept of concurrent engineering and how it can be used to minimize technological uncertainties and minimize end user risk is discussed. The intent of this paper is to provide a basis for discussion of a system and methodologies for managing the technology stock, and optimizing the expenditures on technology development from a laboratory dedicated to fundamental research.

articleTitle: Extending critical knowledge areas: learn, innovate, propagate
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. In the emerging knowledge era segment of the post-industrial epoch, critical knowledge areas (CKAs) represent identifiable bodies of knowledge which are unique to the enterprise. A question begs for response: what is the return on a small percentage increase in the application of intellectual capital, the CKAs? Those who seek to account for asset value have a challenge, the measurement and management of intellectual capital. The new business measure is return on critical knowledge (ROCK). This is a label for the formula that can likely capture the full essence and value of CKAs, and measuring and managing intellectual capital. Strategically aligned human resource systems such as selection, promotion, developing personal and organizational bench strength, compensation, career or role paths, job design and descriptions, job rotation, organizational structuring, CC assessment and the usual plethora of policies accompanying these areas will also contribute to the full delivery of organizational performance and high yield on CKAs.

articleTitle: New MBA bridges business-technology gap
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. There are a number of challenges in the development of an MBA program designed to meet the needs of technology industries. These challenges include: maintaining a balance between business and technology management, integrating the various business functions in the curriculum, maintaining a global and strategic management perspective, and tailoring the program to the specific industries that the program serves. This paper describes the history, development, approach, and experience of a new MBA with specialization in Technology and Innovation Management (TIM). The program has taken more than two years to develop by interacting with a broad cross-section of targeted technology industry professional associations, executives, and prospective students. The program is designed to give students the opportunity to obtain skills in the following areas: strategic and global thinking in technology companies, entrepreneurial and new venture management, innovation and technology change, organizational leadership, managerial decision-making in an environment of rapid technology change, interpersonal communication and team leadership, information systems management, and operations management. The TIM program, in its first year of implementation, has attracted students from both technical and nontechnical academic backgrounds, and has been successful in drawing participants from a broad-base of companies and industries. For the future, the TIM program will need to adapt and change to keep pace with the needs of students and the ever changing nature of the technology industries the program serves.

articleTitle: Selection And Implementation Of Information Technology In The Health Care Industry
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97

articleTitle: Knowledge linkage in international R&D management: the case of Japanese MNCs
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The paper analyzes various types of linkage mechanisms which make it possible for a company to transfer and convert globally-diffused contextual knowledge by looking at the innovative organizational experiments by the Japanese multinational companies which have been considered the most ethnocentric organizations.

articleTitle: Technology innovation management journals: an analysis of citations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper is a citation-analysis based follow-up to the subjective survey conducted in 1993 by the Technology Innovation Management Division (TIMD) of the Academy of Management. The purpose of both studies was to establish a hierarchical rating of journals publishing articles in the field of technology innovation management (TIM).

articleTitle: Cross-functional teams and new product development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. One of the most effective methods for managing complex technology-based new product development efforts is by cross-functional teamwork. Managing a cross-functional team requires considerable skills as effective teamwork is seldom an automatic process. This paper explores the nature of cross-functional teamwork, the issues encountered when a group of talented people attempt cross-disciplinary work, the role of the team leader, characteristics of a team's charter, the team development process for cross-functional teams, and how senior management can support and facilitate the process. Several implications for team leaders are also given.

articleTitle: The development of an organizational transition framework: the application of change models to the Kennedy Space Center
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The contribution of the paper is a framework for organizational transitions involving both changes in mission/role and the number of personnel. The framework is an integration and extension of organizational models, best practices from the literature, interviews from senior executives who experienced significant organizational change, and issues and concerns identified by senior management at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC). KSC as part of the National Aeronautics and Space Association's (NASA) efforts to perform "better, faster, cheaper" has begun a large-scale organizational change effort. The drivers for KSC's transition include: the reduction in NASA's budget, the development a space flight operations contractor (SFOC) for shuttle processing, and a definition of KSC's roles based on NASA's strategic plan. These circumstances lead KSC to undergo a large-scale orderly organizational change. Their effort is similar to the other private, public, and government organizations who have attempted efforts such as downsizing to meet performance requirements. An applied research methodology was designed to ensure a theoretically sound, valid framework was developed which reflected KSC's unique environment, goals, objectives, and concerns because there isn't a universal change model. We propose a model for organizational change which describes the fundamental problem that KSC is experiencing when managing a large-scale transition or change: doing the right work the right way with the right people at the right time. The implications of the model are discussed.

articleTitle: National indicators of technology-based competitiveness: selected results from 1996
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. "High-tech indicators" work at Georgia Tech (USA), begun in 1987, has proceeded through three developmental phases (1988, 1991, 1993), and "graduated" in 1996 from development to periodic production of the indicator series. This paper presents some selected results obtained during the most recent phase of indicator research; emphasis is placed on changes in indicators for particular countries and groups of countries (e.g., the Pacific Rim) since 1993 and the incorporation of several additional countries in the series. Analysis focuses on two general areas: (1) indicators of the future competitiveness of nations (approximately 15 year time horizon); and (2) current ranking of nations on measures of competitiveness in high technology industries, emphasis on high technology production, and rate of change in competitiveness.

articleTitle: The influence of organizational factors on innovation and creativity in US and Japanese high technology firms
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper discusses several organizational factors that influence creativity and innovation in a technical organization. Research suggests that US engineers are more creative in the basic sciences but less productive in the process areas. Japanese R&D engineers appear to be less productive in basic science research, but more creative in research areas related to process control. The influence of group processes, the need to upgrade technical skills and organizational structure help to explain these differences.
