abstract: For any developing country, it is important to accomplish the process from technology importation to assimilation and self-reliant innovation, and it must be aided by the capability-building of indigenous technological innovation. Thus the management of technology in China must include such a strategic issue. This paper, which is based on case studies of Chinese firms, describes the pathways of improvement of indigenous technology innovation capability in the perspective of technology strategy, organizational change and capital support.

articleTitle: Success factors in the management of technological innovations: an efficient implementation concept of technology strategies (based on an empirical study)
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Competition reveals that some enterprises react faster in bringing technological innovations to the market than others. What are the reasons for these differences and how can they be explained? The author has discovered in an empirical study, that the efficiency, with which technology strategies get implemented in enterprises is one of the decisive reasons for this phenomena, The efficient implementation of technology strategies will give the managers of the enterprises the opportunity to bring their technological innovations earlier and more successfully to the market than competitors. This paper discusses an implementation model for technology strategies. The strategic positioning of the technological resources and the management of the core technological competencies of an enterprise, which are necessary for the success of its products, are the central question of the technology strategy. Part of this implementation model is an efficiency concept for the evaluation of the implementation success. In the end, the success of a strategy implementation process is determined by the result. This can be defined as degree of realization of the strategy and is further refined in the manuscript by efficiency criteria. The author differentiates between three categories of efficiency criteria: (1) the general view, (2) the process-oriented view, and (3) the result-oriented view. Recommendations for efficient implementation processes in different implementation situations are included in checklists.

articleTitle: Reducing cycle time by optimizing your product portfolio
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: With companies continually striving to reduce cycle time, on the heels of significant gains, many are finding that further substantial improvement is difficult to achieve, especially on new (or breakthrough) products. This paper discusses factors influencing cycle time and means by which obstacles may be overcome to gain further advantages. Included are ways to gain competitive advantage by coupling product development and product portfolio strategy. The result is a new look at the trade off between the product portfolio and time to market. A benchmark study is presented that demonstrates how product mix can influence cycle time. Once managers understand how their portfolios influence time to market, they have two possible approaches to explore. The first is a set of tools to analyze the portfolio as it relates to risk and development capacity. The second is a set of techniques especially suited for improving the cycle time of new products. Both approaches are recommended for a comprehensive solution to greater competitiveness.

articleTitle: Technological collaboration for sustainable development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: In a rapidly changing, technically complex global economy, firms seek international linkages for the design, development, and deployment of technology. This paper examines the role of technological collaboration in sustainable development through case studies of international projects by Japanese and Canadian firms. Several indicators of a sustainable collaborative relationship (jizoku kanouna kyoryouku kankei) are described.

articleTitle: Management of product development projects in the telecommunication sector
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The article presents the results of part of an empirical survey developed through the study of multiple cases in the telecommunications and antenna sub-sectors of the electronics area. Thirteen projects were selected in twelve different organizations, eleven of which were Brazilian, and one, German. The results suggest that there are a number of similarities regarding management practices adopted by the sector, implying a trend towards consolidation of a typical management culture for the sector. Descriptions are presented and discussed regarding some of the main relationships between the planning process and project performance.

articleTitle: Technology decisions for a flexible health care organization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The fastest growing service sector, health care, is facing the same challenges as their manufacturing counterparts. In this case, however, there are more constraints since health care is partially regulated by the government and reimbursing organizations. These constraints and intensive competition forced health care organizations to revise their strategic objectives. Similarities of the new competitive challenges encouraged health care organizations to look at new technologies used in dealing with these challenges in the manufacturing sector. Health care organizations have a number of strategic choices in meeting their customer requirements. These choices can be summarized in a strategy continuum defined by two extreme strategies: broad range competition and specialist competition. In order to compete in an environment which is defined by new consumer driven focus in which new products and services must be developed quickly and marketed continuously with reasonable cost, health care organizations, just like their manufacturing counterparts have been doing it, must adopt flexible organization systems. This is a strategic move by both types of organizations. There are significant organizational requirements to be met in this transition. Role of technology, organization's strategic emphasis, their current resource-mix and capacity availability, market pressures, government regulations, and ever complex reimbursement mechanism will add additional constraints in this transformation. Flexible organizations for health care will be a requirement for survival.

articleTitle: Staying ahead of the competition: technology acquisition and its global implications
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The results of the research project on technology acquisition in the electronics industry of Oregon are presented in this paper. The objective of the projects was to identify the alternatives used for technology acquisition and then to explain the implications of the various alternatives which are: existing/new; internal R&D; licensing; joint ventures; corporate; venturing; and strategic alliances.

articleTitle: A SOFT science and technology framework for international R&D project with organization mix
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This study focuses on international R&D projects with organization mix, i.e., heterogeneous parties namely government, corporation and academia. For such a scenario, the authors propose a framework incorporating world view and system concepts. The framework is shown to be practical by an example of a collaborative R&D project of Asia Pacific countries.

articleTitle: Case-study of a Virtual Project Office for a systems integrator
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The nature and use of management models to analyze a systems integration firm are described and the resultant setup of a Virtual Project Office (VPO) is outlined. Business and organizational benefits that arose are reported together with lessons about the models' role in facilitating rapid organizational change and performance improvement.

articleTitle: Management of focused storage technology in a hybrid job-shop environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper describes focused storage inventory control and discusses a current case involving the implementation of focused storage concepts and technology in a hybrid job-shop environment. The paper covers technology management issues faced by the job-shop that uses focused storage and those faced by the researcher/consultant proposing such a system.

articleTitle: Work force diversity: employee attitudes and perceptions
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Approximately 45 percent of all net additions to the US labor force in the 1990s will be nonwhite and almost two-thirds will be female. Half of the nonwhite additions will be first generation immigrants, mostly from Asian and Latin American countries. Therefore, it is becoming increasingly important for companies to encourage workforce diversity in order to better compete in the future. This study was the first stage of a process to evaluate the status and to measure the progress of one organization regarding managing diversity. In this report, a survey was developed with the following objectives: (1) to estimate employee attitudes toward diversity; (2) to estimate employee perceptions of the company's support for diversity; (3) to track, over time, the effectiveness of diversity training programs; and (4) to compare employee attitudes with those of employees of other companies. To accomplish this, an anonymous survey was developed and distributed to a random sample of 200 employees. The results were compared with published national results by John P. Fernandez.

articleTitle: Coupling of technology management and strategic planning processes: the state of the art
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. This research is the result of a particularly productive and unusual partnership between academics and practitioners and is part of an ongoing research program where many of the concepts and frameworks continue to evolve. With the cooperation of a consortium, the National Center for Manufacturing Sciences (NCMS), a half-dozen large technology-oriented organizations have been participating in the research, providing information through numerous site visits and dozens of interviews. In addition to this traditional data gathering effort, however, the research program has benefited from having key participants from the organizations provide critiques and refinements to the process-based framework as it emerged from the fieldwork and from the literature. The researchers and practitioners working on this study jointly identified a large number of technology management processes as part of an overall framework for the management of technology. This framework is based on a process-based view of organizations, where a process is defined as a set of related activities or routines. For each process within this overall framework, the authors have developed as part of the research effort: a brief description; key issues related to the process; potential best practices; ways in which academics or practitioners have tried to measure the process; relationships to other processes; and references to the literature.

articleTitle: Technology transfer: an agency theoretic model
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The relationships among different types of innovations in an organization seem to have received very little research attention. An understanding of their relationships over the life cycle of a technology would help firms to not only prepare for changes, but also to plan and allocate its scarce resources effectively. This paper presents a conceptual model that integrates earlier research on different types of innovations and hypothesizes relationships among them.

articleTitle: The motivation of innovators to form informal communication networks
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Networking has become an important part of the innovation process. New product formulation teams have used systematic informal networking with innovators in the information technology industry in order to formulate new product ideas. It has been questioned as to why these innovators agree to informally network with these teams. This study examined the motivation behind innovators agreeing to network with others in their industry. Data from 103 innovators in the imaging technology industry was collected. Ninety (87%) of the innovators contacted agreed to informally network in the scenario presented. The agreeing innovators were classified using the following model: leading edge suppliers versus those that had instigated informal networking before (proactive innovators) versus those that had not instigated informal networking before (reactive innovators). Significant differences were found between the motivations of leading edge suppliers, proactive innovators, and reactive innovators. The implications for new product development teams are outlined.

articleTitle: Market entry strategies of small automotive suppliers
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Global opportunities in the auto industry have resulted in increases in production outside North America. This paper reports the results of a study in which a group of small automotive suppliers assessed the appropriateness of global entry strategies, and evaluated the degree of asset specificity and risks.

articleTitle: Getting innovative academic research products to the marketplace successfully
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Universities are developing highly innovative technological products, without any commercial outlets. Customers in the marketplace demand new innovative products that will astonish, delight and surprise them. Innovation and technology management are key ingredients in university engineering product design courses. An innovation process model has been applied and developed further to form a technology transfer process model. If this is followed and coupled with a coherent strategic plan, this will ensure that these innovative technological products will be successful in the marketplace.

articleTitle: The DOTSS (developer-off-the-shelf systems) approach: a progress report
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper presents a progress report of ongoing research into, and marketing of, the developer-off-the-shelf systems (DOTSS) approach relative to the acquisition of information technology. The DOTSS procedure and concept is reiterated along with various terms of the ITMRA of 1996. Additional issues explored include DOTSS-related barriers, technology transfer and notions of leverage.

articleTitle: Technology acquisition and utilization in metal goods
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper analyzes the technology acquisition and utilization process in metal goods manufacturing organizations through a survey instrument which is conducted in the Mid-West region of the US. The goal of this study is to identify the channels, types, reasons, impacts, difficulties, and limitations of technology acquisition and utilization process in metal goods sector.

articleTitle: Recycling technology-a short cut to new business creation in software companies
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: New business creation is usually perceived as a complex and time consuming process filled with obstacles. Yet, this paper demonstrates that new business creation in software companies may come about quickly if they exploit the equivocality of the information technology and their interpretive capabilities to recycle existing software applications and enter new business areas.

articleTitle: The institutional dynamics of information technology transfer: a comparative case analysis
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper examines the institutional dynamics of information technology transfer with particular emphasis on the roles of publicly funded centres for research and development. The theoretical model serves as a basis for qualitative case analysis and comparison of research management structures in two Canadian research centres. Recommendations for an appropriate research methodology are formulated.

articleTitle: Vocational training and the innovation process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Innovations need new organisation of vocational training. Referring to innovation cycle theory and network economics, the paper analyses empirical data and proposals for reforms of vocational training and innovations (Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Japan). Three types of institutions and enterprises-innovative, adaptable and hesitative, innovation process phases and innovation policy measures are pointed out.

articleTitle: Virtual R&D organisations: lessons from the pharmaceutical industry
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: In this paper, the virtual organisation of R&D in Pharmaceuticals is studied. A virtual R&D organisation is designed to access the external knowledge and resources necessary for innovation. Different criteria are needed for managing the virtual organisation of research and of development activities. This is a key issue to ensure successful collaborations.

articleTitle: An economy risk analysis of installed capacity expansion at the Three Gorges Power Plant
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. This paper studies the possibility and economy of peak regulation operation during flood period at the Three Gorges reservoir, which will at the same time satisfy the requirements for comprehensive utilization such as flood control, sediment sluicing and navigation, and proposes that if the installed capacity of the Three Gorges Power Plant is to be expanded from the designed 18.2 million kW to 22.4 million kW, the nonregulation operation of the power plant will become regulation operation during flood period, thus increasing greatly the capacity benefits of the power plant, and strengthening the operation flexibility and economy of the power system. Because of the Three Gorges Project's enormous dimension, wide scope of influence and numerous uncertain (risk) factors involved, this paper presents a model for economy risk analysis on the basis of the maximum entropy in accordance with the information entropy principle, and derives the probabilistic density distribution function of six major economic indexes which are of the minimum prejudice, and based on the distribution function established. An economic risk analysis is made for the Three Gorges Project.

articleTitle: Integrated management of technology
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper deals with the integration of product development and technology development in industrial corporations. First, case studies of a look at how four case firms go about integrating their product and technology development, are presented. Based on this, a definition of this kind of integration is proposed along with a model for describing different ways to integrate product and technology development.

articleTitle: The congruence imperative [personnel management]
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. The Ascent of Man continues and can be described as a global search for higher achievement. Higher achievement requires the contribution of individual experts to collaborative problem solving. The organizational goal is for individuals who are working near their top potential, who are satisfied with their assignment and have found personal goals that are congruent with the goals of the organization. These goals are most often met by challenging assignments. For managers, congruence means holding on to their top performers in the competition between productivity and personal growth. For individuals, self-leadership is required because empowerment has shifted the responsibility for problem solving from managers to the problem solvers. The leadership exercised by managers facilitates the process required for synergistic achievement. Success is in the hands of those who also implement. This becomes a partnership, a search for congruence in which the productivity needs of the enterprise are met, and the personal growth of the individual is sustained.

articleTitle: Global versus the Indian industry's competitive edge with flexible manufacturing technology
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Flexible manufacturing systems (FMSs) have already demonstrated their formidable impact on the global competitiveness of modern manufacturing industries. Adaptation of flexible manufacturing technology (FMT) is considered essential to retain the competitive edge in the context of rapidly reducing half life of technologies and products. The study presents the Indian scenario in this context. The potential of FMT diffusion in India is assessed with respect to the other leading global players.

articleTitle: Re-engineering people through leadership and empowerment: a case study
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The authors present the challenges experienced by Velden Engineering (UK) Ltd, during their pursuit of total quality management (TQM). The company's efforts were channelled through their nontraditional approach to employee training. This approach has clearly demonstrated an improvement in organisational and employee performance, and goes beyond the traditions of conventional skills training, by addressing the educational development needs of all employees. This integrated strategy has been formulated through re-engineering the people process and by integrating leadership and empowerment into the corporate culture. The concept of strict management discipline within Velden has been replaced by that of leadership: giving up compulsory control-gaining influence, co-operation, trust, and commitment. Velden's old determinist approach to management has changed. It is now one of building knowledge, people and teams within the organisation, and integrating employees together, to achieve a common purpose and provide fulfilment for those involved. The entire Velden workforce is lead from the front by a chief executive officer, who inspires the whole workforce. However, in order to ensure continued prosperity and growth, Velden strives to ensuring that everybody within the organisation develops their leadership qualities to their full potential.

articleTitle: Collaborative support environment for organizational innovativeness
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. We present preliminary results of the project INNOVISIO, which aims for support of organizational innovativeness in a contract research laboratory. In such an environment, new innovations are the object of everyday activities, and the demand for innovativeness is both emphasized and complicated. The overall objective of the project is: (1) to increase the sensitivity of the organization for new innovations; (2) to identify and experiment platforms for processing of new ideas; and (3) to set up a repository for ideas, tools and supporting material. According to our previous experience, a "creativity manifesto" has only a temporary effect on innovativeness. To overcome this, our approach is to introduce a cultural change through defined procedures, aiming for identifying and exploring new ideas. Our focus is on concrete methods and procedures for idea generation, on creation and maintaining an accessible repository of ideas and knowledge, and on techniques for idea verification and exploration. First experiences of creativity techniques, intranet and of an associated virtual reality prototyping project are presented. Information technology provides means to define and standardize organizational procedures. We foresee applications for idea and knowledge repository and for idea exploration methods. Creativity techniques can be used as an auxiliary aid. Intranet should be used as an integrating concept, although some technical challenges remain to be solved. Resources for further development of new ideas and potential innovations are allocated using a "virtual enterprise" framework.

articleTitle: Collaboration issues in the implementation of new technology: a study in change management
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Implementation of new technology is most effective when a systemic change management program is adopted. A case study provides an example with statistical information to support the hypothesis.

articleTitle: Dimensions of technological developments across different phases of the product life cycle-an explorative study in the Indian machine building sector
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: This paper reports the findings of a survey, aimed at understanding the dimensions of technological developments (TDs) in different phases of the product life cycle (PLC). The study is based on a survey done in a sample of Indian machinery manufacturing organisations in the context of the economic liberalisation in India which has allowed free imports of technology and goods. This has brought about a greater need for continuous TDs to obtain sustainable competitive benefits throughout the PLC. Various dimensions of TDs were obtained through a factor analysis and the results suggested the relative importance of the dimensions of TDs varied according to the phase of the PLC.

articleTitle: Communication and cooperation in a virtual design space
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. A major problem in the management of a product development process is to facilitate the continuous communication between perspectives of different stakeholder groups, especially in early phases of design. In this paper we suggest that virtual prototypes-3D models of product prototypes with functionality in virtual reality-are a promising candidate to form the core of a support system that smoothly integrates several of the necessary support functions for multidisciplinary cooperation in design into one system. Thus, we address the question what should be communicated between the different stakeholders in a design situation from the point of view of Activity Theory, an approach well known in the fields of computer supported cooperative work (CSCW) and human computer interaction (HCI). Consequently, in addition to the virtual prototype as a common object for supporting cooperation between designers, we identify the following four means for cooperation: by directly changing the state of the object of the cooperative work, through a jointly constructed common information space, through a specially designed coordination mechanism or by active communication between persons through communication channels. Each of these means needs a different kind of computer support, and their importance varies during the design process. We elaborate the concept of virtual prototype into a concept of virtual design space, which could be an environment that integrates these perspectives of cooperation and communication support for a design group.

articleTitle: Development of a multi-disciplinary framework for studying generation of new product concepts
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Success in new product development (NPD) is increasingly associated with the proficiency of steps carried out prior to entering the development phase. Concept generation is the step that establishes alternatives and defines a workable concept. This step appears to be the linchpin of the concept development phase. Factors representing the social, organizational, cognitive, and conceptual design elements of NPD converge during this step. It is the point where market information, strategic plans, and technological details must be balanced by a small group of people who must represent the collective capability of a firm. The authors' proposed framework, which link these factors together, offers an interpretation for common shortcomings reported during the concept development phase.

articleTitle: Data envelopment analysis with integral targets [management decision making]
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Data envelopment analysis (DEA) inherently assumes that the feasible targets for inputs and outputs are continuous. This paper develops and illustrates extensions to DEA that allow for integer valued inputs and outputs. It is found that DEA's implicit assumption of continuous targets can be significant in certain applications.

articleTitle: Economic and technical rationalism in engineering education
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Economic rationalism may be aligned with developments in a "deep-holistic" approach to learning. Such an approach is perceived as the antithesis of technical rationalism in education. Against such a background, the paper explores the management of trade-offs between "deep" versus "holistic" educational approaches in engineering education for life-long learning.

articleTitle: Intelligent computer-aided instructional systems: ready for prime time?
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: For an organization to achieve and retain global status and leadership through technology management, its educational and training systems must also be "world class." This paper provides a brief overview of intelligent computer-aided instructional (ICAI) systems and reaches a conclusion that they are not yet ready for "prime time".

articleTitle: Lessons learned implementing ISO 9001 in a software organization
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: There are no short cuts for a software development company in reaching ISO 9001 certification. The organizational culture of a software development company does not fit well with a traditional cross-functional core team model. Instead, a model of close partnering with individual product development teams can lead to ISO 9001 registration in a value-added way.

articleTitle: Regional program to promote technology transfer from the public sector to the private sector: Japanese experience
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The authors analyzed the individual programs and the specified successful projects of the typical institutes in the public sector. They propose the common conceptual scheme of technology transfer from the public sector to the private sector through the analysis. They point out some problems concerning the technology transfer for small and medium-sized enterprises (SME) and propose some ideas of how to solve them.

articleTitle: Prioritizing strategic issues using quadratic goal programming
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Many techniques have been used to develop priorities, or weights, for a set of decision-making factors. These include multidimensional scaling, regression analysis, analytic hierarchy process, mathematical programming and Logit. In this paper, the "factors" are considered to be the relevant decision issues in strategic planning. A quadratic goal programming approach for determining the weights for a set of strategic issues is presented. The procedure starts with pair-wise comparison ratings that are derived by using triads of the issues.

articleTitle: Forecasting techniques using fuzzy set theory
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. In this paper, we studied Delphi method, exponential smoothing, moving-average, and least-squares method by using fuzzy set theory. The procedure followed in Delphi method is to solicit and collate opinions about a certain subjects from experts and feed back digested appraisals to narrow the differences among opinions until a near agreement is obtained. Kaufmann describes a Delphi method using triangular fuzzy numbers. In his didactic example, Kaufmann considers a technological progress well specified and makes an inquiry with twelve experts. Every expert gives the earliest date, the date of maximum of presumption, and the latest date for the technological progress considered. Then, the mean and the deviations from the mean are computed. The experts are informed and return their respective values with the possibility of some changes. The process continue until the analysts find a stability. In exponential smoothing method, a weighting factor that gives more or less prominence to recent happenings is selected. The moving-average method predicts the demand for the next period from the average demand experienced during several recent periods. The least-square method can be used to determine the line of best fit to plotted data points. In the case of fuzziness, we use a sequence of interval of confidence instead of a sequence of ordinary numbers of actual demand. This is because we assume that we don't have exact and reliable data of old demand to use in the least-squares method.

articleTitle: Competition, strategic technology options and game theory in science and technology policy: the SEMATECH-Sandia National Laboratories partnership
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: The semiconductor industry consortium SEMATECH is used as the platform to study and critique science and technology policy on high tech consortia. The concepts of leveraging strategic technology options and competing in a game-theoretic context drive the analysis and research done. The authors focus especially on the collaborative R&D efforts undertaken by Sematech and Sandia National Laboratories.

articleTitle: The informal structure of project organizations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Project management is a process of completing a one time activity with a set of well defined end results described by scope, quality, time and cost, with and through the actions of others. To achieve project end results, an efficient and effective project organization structure that facilitates communication flows and cooperation among internal employees and with external stakeholders is necessary. This paper describes the whole process of selecting the right project leadership using Krackhardt and Hanson's mapping technique of employees' informal relationships. The paper elaborates the mapping results of networks in matrix formats. It is illustrated by the same case study used by Krackhardt and Hanson. This shows how to best select the project manager based on all employees input, not by one CEO's personal assumption and observation.

articleTitle: Research of information impact to Japanese company
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. In Japanese companies, since the bubble economy collapse, management action is observed with a remarkable BPR and restructuring promotion. As for the promotion of making the information network and the open management development by it, the last effect of the management rebuilding is expected on the inside. The Internet is the first on the list as a representative in the network with the function of the transmission of information of the multimedia type. The barrier of the data layout difference is detached and the influence power on the management of the Internet and the intranet which can be constructed comparatively easily besides cannot be overlooked. Of course, the effort of the network construction has been done in Japan since the former. The expansion of so-called outsourcing is progressing in Japan. A big change which not since postwar days is taking place in current Japanese style management. Does the appearance of a Japanese company in the future only follow that of the US firm? Or, can a Japanese company acquire an original management style? And, to what problem does the management of a Japanese company being faced now? For the beginning of what solution is a Japanese company growing? This paper is stated around these subjects.

articleTitle: Human element and productivity improvement: converging manufacturing strategies towards an effective strategy
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Capability improvement is now one the crucial targets within every manufacturing strategy. This is due to high competitive environments within industrial institutions. Despite various changes and vast technological automation in production systems the 'human element' is still placed at the heart of any successful manufacturing system. In fact, the strategy for keeping continuous productivity improvement in engineering and technology management has been crucial for enterprises and countries over the last decade. Many attempts have been made to reduce the operating role of the human element within the process of industrial production. This experience, along with insufficient attention on the issue of 'human factors', caused a number of failures. The author believes that by integration of the most successful techniques and strategies (i.e. total quality control (TQC), just in time (JIT), factory automation (FA) and total production maintenance (TPM)) used in advanced manufacturing systems, productivity improvement, innovation, and technological systems effectiveness will be accelerated. The focus is on the human side of manufacturing systems. It will lead us to identify an effective conceptual approach for the establishment of appropriate strategy which includes the key element of "continuous productivity improvement".

articleTitle: International forecasting use of management models
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Management models, when augmented by factors not normally considered domestically and used within a broader framework, can better explain and forecast strategic developments in foreign countries. Presented are: models and factors to consider; illustrative results for Hungary; and a return/risk optimizing technology transfer model for application elsewhere.

articleTitle: Human resource development in the re-engineered corporation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. This paper addresses the impacts on human resource development in the re-engineered telecommunications industry, especially the Regional Bell Operating Companies (RBOC) and how the Bellcore Training and Educational organization and other technical training organizations are meeting the needs of this new environment Telecommunications corporations like US WEST, have re-engineered their processes to where fewer employees are doing more functions with many employees located in "mega-centers". The new method of operation creates new demands for training and delivery options.

articleTitle: A model program with emphasis on working experience and linkage to industries for manufacturing engineering students
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Manufacturing engineering is to determine and define machinery, tools, and processes to transform raw materials into products through the use of efficient methods. Students in this field need theoretical knowledge and practical skills. The best way for training students is to cooperate with enterprises. This paper describes a successful model program for manufacturing engineering. Students who have entered a manufacturing engineering program for two years need to take a competency test to ensure that they have adequate basic technology. After students pass the competency test, they spend one more year of study in professional technology. Once students finish professional technology courses, they are assigned to enterprises for at least three months. For students to demonstrate their ability integrating theory and practice, they need to take two courses in their senior year: project design/fabrication and technical report. Problems to be solved for these two courses should be found from enterprises. In other words, there are three stages for students to finish their courses of study: competency test, working in industry, and project design/fabrication with technical report. Through this program, students become highly potential for their professional career.

articleTitle: Technology management in Indian automobile industry-Hero Honda experience
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Indian Automobile Industry is passing through a phase of rapid transition. Technology transfer is taking place from leading automobile manufacturing countries in the world. A case study of Hero Honda Motors Limited (HHML) has been presented covering major strategic technology management issues with special focus on technology transfer arrangement, subsequent absorption, and innovations made in product and process technologies by local technologists. The case study presented here is a part of an empirical study being carried out in Indian automobile industry to assess the technology management practices in the firms of developing countries in general and in India in particular. The article also proposes a framework for designing technology strategy for a firm in a developing country.

articleTitle: The management of innovation and technology in the automotive industry: a focus upon Rover Group Ltd
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Innovation is a basic necessity of successful organizations to gain competitive advantage through continuous improvement and the bringing of products to the market quicker, cheaper and better than their competition. The automotive industry has become a true global supply business and effective monopolies are being rapidly replaced to improve competitiveness. The reliance upon traditional methods and technologies, the dependence upon competitors to innovate and the rapid copying of the resulting methodologies and technology through the adoption of "fast follow" strategies may have short term financial benefits. However, the removal of innovation exhibits serious medium and long term detriment to the business and prevents world class performance. Within Rover Group, senior management has become increasingly aware that it must develop an innovation culture to survive.

articleTitle: Influence of technology on product development process
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. It is a commonly accepted notion that a product development process (PDP) depends upon at least three key basic elements: organizational design; people and prevailing culture; and technology. Each element influences the PDP differently and to varying degrees, based upon the element's characteristics and associated time constant (i.e., the time it requires to take root and begin exerting influence in a significant manner). This paper mainly examines ways in which technology influences the PDP. Within that context, it then considers how the pace of technology evolution (slow, medium and fast) potentially impacts the product development process. It then addresses the issues related to investments required for the deployment of technology for process improvement. Finally, it examines the bounds or limits of technological influence on the PDP in terms of cost reduction and lead time.

articleTitle: Creating 'win-win' university/industry relationships
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. As federal funds become tighter, university researchers will seek industrial sponsorship more often. Satisfying an industrial sponsor is often more difficult than satisfying a federal sponsor. An industrial sponsor's purpose for funding research is typically to solve an immediate local issue. Consequently, the industrial sponsored researcher must ensure that research findings will improve the sponsor's current problem. To do this will require researchers to become more involved in implementation. Solving an immediate problem is not the primary objective of most researchers though. It is to create and disseminate new knowledge. To develop successful university/industry partnerships, each phase of the research process must integrate both researcher and practitioner objectives. A critical first step of the process is bringing industrial leaders and researchers together. The Socio-technical Alliance for Industrial Research (STAIR) at Virginia Tech is an example of a mechanism which brings researchers and practitioners together for mutual benefit. Industrial leaders attend bi-annual forums held on campus where they network with peers and researchers. Researchers are exposed to current industrial issues. Funding, access, or consulting have been outcomes from the STAIR forums. Key learnings we have had in relationship building with industrial leaders include: design the research component into the proposal or contract, establishing the research a component of the project; build credibility in helping solve the industrial issue prior to negotiating the research requirements; establish implementation expectations early; and approach consulting projects cautiously if rigorous research methodology is a goal.

articleTitle: Experiences from facilitating the design and implementation of performance measurement systems-the influence of the team and its leader
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The importance of performance measurement is growing as organisations move from financial to nonfinancial measures, attempt to improve longer term business results though alignment of the company with its strategy and concentrate their effort on what really matters to improve performance. Frameworks for performance measurement such as the balanced business scorecard and the SMART performance pyramid are increasingly being discussed and used. But although these frameworks are useful in themselves, it is important to understand the process of populating the framework, deciding exactly what to measure, why, when and how? The processes to do this usually include facilitated workshops as an important component and this paper addresses this aspect within one particular process.

articleTitle: Fitness for transfer: improving the international transfer of manufacturing capability
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Knowing how well a manufacturing process will fit a new location prior to its transfer is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for predicting transfer problems. This paper argues that firms must also consider how easy a manufacturing process is to transfer. A pre-transfer tool, tested here in multiple case studies, uses the dimensions of location fit and ease of transfer to provide a means of measuring the fitness for transfer of a firm's manufacturing processes.

articleTitle: Taiwan's and university co-operation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: In order to understand the current practice of university-industry (U&I) co-operation in education and training, consulting services, testing services and research and development (R&D), a survey was conducted and followed with interviews in this study. The results of this study can be used as the basis to improve U&I co-operation.

articleTitle: The effects of CASE on software production in UK organizations
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: CASE (computer aided software engineering) software improves developer productivity and applications software quality compared with 4GL and 3GL technologies. Easier and less maintenance contributes to enhanced productivity, and partly reflects improvements to software reliability, accuracy and capability. Management priorities and practices also affect software production, with participative management styles proving most effective.

articleTitle: Military to private sector technology transfer: a research agenda
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: In the last fifteen years, there has been an increasing emphasis on transferring Department of Defense technology to the private sector. In this paper, the author presents an overview of research he has conducted concerning various aspects of this type of technology transfer and proposes avenues for future research.

articleTitle: Research and development as seen from a "PATRA" point of view
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: A framework named "poly-agent theory of reference activities (PATRA)" is suggested. The authors apply this framework to Japanese-style research and development (R&D) systems. They discuss why Japanese engineers and scientists prefer incremental R&D to fundamental or radical R&D. The authors found an example of macro information produced by a higher-order agent (the corporation) changing internal models of lower-order agents (engineers and scientists).

articleTitle: Identifying the cost implications of manufacturing IT/IS investments
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. As organizational investments in information technology (IT) and information systems (IS) continue to grow, significant amounts of capital need justifying. However, many companies are increasingly reporting their inability to justify their investment in IT/IS because of the nature of costs and benefits associated with its implementation. The reason for this is because many organizational budgeting processes rely on financially orientated appraisal techniques as an integral part of the decision making process. These accountancy frameworks are often used to assess the 'bottomline' financial impact of an investment, by setting tangible project costs against those quantifiable benefits and savings predicted to be achievable. However, traditional appraisal techniques are considered to be no longer appropriate in justifying investments in IT/IS because of the nature of intangible benefits, together with the complexity of direct and indirect cost implications. Hence, the predictive value in using many traditional investment appraisal techniques is increasingly being questioned. The authors in this paper identify the full range of cost implications associated with the adoption of IT/IS, with a particular focus on manufacturing resource planning (MRPII). These cost implications are then developed into a taxonomy of direct and indirect costs that clearly need consideration during the justification process.

articleTitle: Structural adaptation and technological entrepreneurship in Taiwan's industrial development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Taiwan's technological development illustrates a model of government-guided and knowledge-linked industrial networks. Technological entrepreneurship in Taiwan displays a framework in which knowledge effectively flows through government-subsidized research and spin-off to industries. Taiwan's high-tech industries are shaping their competitive advantages by restructuring internal organizations and repositioning strategic paths.

articleTitle: Roadblocks to productivity improvement in the semiconductor industry
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Semiconductor manufacturing is one of the most complicated production environments for such reasons as: reentrant product flows; variant batching; clean room environments (imposing constraints on the layout and operations); complicated equipment to fix; and inherent conflict between the need for customized products on the one hand, and high volume, low cost production on the other. Opportunities for productivity improvement, what the authors call "visions of excellence in semiconductor manufacturing" are hindered by these roadblocks. They propose some indicators for the identification of each of the top five roadblocks and the possible industrial engineering solutions for tackling each of them. These top five roadblocks have been identified based on their industry experience and the interviews they have had with many managers in the semiconductor industry.

articleTitle: Narrativity and a way for multimedia contents creation support
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. With the advance of multimedia technology, effective ways to support contents creation process in organizations are expected. As one of the essential characteristics of multimedia service is attained by the systematic ability to flexibly create a variety of contents according to different requirements which various consumers have. Thus the support of contents creation process is needed. By making use of strong knowledge bases, inference mechanisms, multimedia functions in computer technology, systematic support for narrative creation process becomes possible. Here, we regard the structure of multimedia contents as a kind of narrative in a broad sense, and we propose a conceptual and fundamental idea on narrative-based contents creation support. We have formalized the mechanisms by artificial intelligence technology. In this case, we don't think that narrative structure limits the diversity.

articleTitle: Implications for management in 2005 and beyond
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. The influences from technology, education, the socioeconomic system, organizational trends, and the globalization of the marketplace, workforce and corporation, will affect management in the year 2005 and beyond. In 2005, enabling technologies will eliminate middle management's role of collecting, organizing, filtering and disseminating information throughout the organization. Managers must become corporate change agents, knowledgeable of technology and possessing the ability to use technology to gain a sustainable competitive advantage. The authors argue that a sustainable competitive advantage can only be achieved when a company's workforce learns, thinks, creates, invents and establishes new levels of quality, faster than their competitors.

articleTitle: Using influence diagrams for PERT
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. We describe a new method for explicit modeling of decisions that bear on activity times in a project. This method extends the PERT belief network (PBN) model to include decisions variables. The resulting network is called PERT Influence Diagram (PID). A PID is a PBN that includes decision variables, where arrows into decision nodes mean that the decision maker knows the value at each of the decision node's predecessors. A PBN uses belief networks (BNs) to model dependence between completion and duration times, where a BN is a directed acyclic graph in which nodes represent variables, and arrows represent probabilistic dependencies which are quantified by conditional distributions. A PBN extends the traditional PERT network model to include not only duration times, but also other chance variables that affect duration and completion times. We assume that the product of all marginal and conditional distributions specifies the joint density of all variables in a PID. We use a combination of stochastic dynamic programming and Gibbs sampling, an iterative Monte Carlo method, to solve PIDs. We solve PIDs by determining the decision strategy that minimizes the expected completion time of the project. We also compute, for every strategy, the mean completion time of the project and the probability of completing the project within a specified time. We illustrate our ideas with an example of a software development project. In summary, PIDs enhance managerial decision making by allowing project managers to explicitly model decision and chance variables that bear on activity times in a project.

articleTitle: Team goal setting to reduce employee isolation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only as given. Leadership through effective team goal setting techniques reduces isolation. Isolation is a real-life problem experienced by many managers today. This problem is becoming more prevalent as technology advances. Face to face communication diminishes as more workers telecommute and business expands internationally. Managers have an obligation to apply tools and models that have demonstrated significant personal and corporate advantages to managing in isolation. This paper examines two corporate cases that use the team goal setting process to achieve outstanding results. Different techniques are discussed demonstrating that leading in isolation is a choice that will no longer deliver results required to compete in an international marketplace.

articleTitle: Challenging complexity: planning and implementing advanced technology in the factory of the future
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Even though traditional "smokestack industries" have the reputation as technological backwaters compared to today's information-based industries, many have been undergoing a quiet transformation that has resulted in significant new approaches to technology management. The author describes how the redesign of traditional manufacturing processes offers a unique opportunity to rethink the approach to process design and management. There is compelling evidence that simpler designs often are better.

articleTitle: Incubator program in Taiwan [new businesses]
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. In Taiwan's industry, the small and medium enterprises play leading roles in economic development, being flexible in management, able to attend the needs of the markets, and capable of manufacturing diverse products on a small scale. However, Taiwan has limited land for industrial use, the raised labor cost and environmental protection cost, which gets more attention, increases the management cost that gradually convert small and medium enterprises from their traditional labor-intensive industry to technology-intensive industry with more competitive advantage. It is really a challenge for them to get their industry upgraded, due to the difficulty in getting new technology in addition to their limited scale, capital, and human resources. The establishment of incubators will mark the beginning of a new era in Taiwan. Incubators can provide new entrepreneurs an excellent environment for business incubations, lower the risk while commercializing an innovative technology, at the same time, contributing to the integration of technology resources. In order to make Taiwan's second economic miracle possible, new ventures are encouraged to develop innovative technology with added value, an aim to changing Taiwan to be a technology island, at the same time, an Asia Pacific Operation Center. Up to April 1997, eight university based incubators, two nonprofit research institution-based incubators and one private incubator have been established since 1996. This research focuses on one of the effective ways to upgrade the technologies of small and medium enterprises as well as the orientation, content, and planning and progress of incubators in Taiwan.

articleTitle: Technological innovation and computed aided thinking: project oriented curricula and engineering management program
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Classical scientific and engineering work is changing due to computers, software and the information highway. Computers and software packages are used for scientific, engineering and administrative work. Innovation and creativity can also be supported by some systematic approach and software. Software for CAT (computed aided thinking) is used for heuristic creative innovation in the course of technological innovation. Innovation's results are evaluated and compared from the point of view classical approach versus software supported approach. Project management courses give students the other important knowledge of how to manage technology. Project oriented curricula concentrated in innovation are analyzed after three years of student's and faculty's experience. Project oriented curricula as a transdisciplinary (multidisciplinary) program are discussed with relationship to the engineering management program. The real examples of student's innovation are presented.

articleTitle: The policies and measures and methods of cooperation between industry, academic and scientific research institutes in China
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Due to the effect of long-term structural planning, Chinese firms lacked in their research and development capabilities. Although colleges, universities and scientific research institutes possessed enormous potentiality in this area, however their research tended to lay particular stress on basic research. Under the social conditions of the present market economy, technology is increasingly becoming a key factor influencing corporate competitiveness. This requires strengthening the cooperation between industry, academic, and scientific research institutes in the areas of research and development. As China attempts to carry out its structural reform, the need for such cooperation is particularly imminent. Consequently since the early 1980s the government of China has actively promoted the cooperation between such institution in their R&D efforts. The cooperation between industry, academic and scientific research institutes in China is characterized by the following methods: technology transfer; contractual research and development which can be further divided into development by consignment and development by contract; cooperation through the establishment of joint research and development institutions; and establishing joint stock companies using the combined funds of enterprise, academic and scientific research institutions. The technology is valued in registered capital. Other methods include companies which provide funding to universities research institutions for the training and saving problems that may exist in the companies technology or production facilities etc.

articleTitle: New product development (NPD) in high tech environments: a case study
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. NPD has been one of the most studied research fields in recent years. The research efforts have been shared by academic institutes and companies. One of the main industries where NPD has become critical is the electronics industry. A main characteristic of this industry is continuously reducing product life cycles. This is both a result of a changing environment and is effecting the environment to change further. Cooper has extensively studied NPD over the years. His research findings indicate significant trends being adopted in high tech companies to be implemented into their NPD practices. One of the important trends is using the gate system to distinguish among different phases in NPD, a process discussed in the case presented in this paper. The company studied is a division of a Fortune 500 company, manufacturing computer motherboards. Many trends cited in the literature were adopted in the case company. There were also some variations from general NPD structures in the case company, such as the significantly short product life cycles created an NPD organization where NPD and maintenance teams work together on products.

articleTitle: Measuring manufacturing performance: dimensions and OEE
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. It is not obvious how organisations should measure overall manufacturing performance (OMP). Various approaches with a large number of measures on different hierarchical levels exist. The objectives of the paper are to define dimensions of effective OMP, to analyse the fulfilment of these dimensions in a case study and, in two field studies, analyse how the overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) measure contributes to measurement of OMP.

articleTitle: The use of systems integration architecture (SIA) to facilitate collaboration within and along the supply chain
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. The area of interest is the use of SIA to provide easy-to-use advanced technologies to facilitate collaboration within and along the supply chain, based upon AAMRC companies which require the integration of functions from disparate applications used in message passing protocols along the supply chain (protocols include CORBA, http/java, rpc, OLE, Distributed OLE and COM).

articleTitle: Towards a framework of engineering management disciplines
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. A suitable framework can provide a useful description or definition of the term engineering management and the body of knowledge implied. Such a framework of subjects and disciplines could be useful in designing engineering management educational programs. The first aspect of engineering management is the management of technology. This clearly forms part of the strategic management of the enterprise. Secondly, co-ordination and integration of engineering activities form part of the task of the engineering manager. These activities are defined within the product life cycle that is depicted in this paper.

articleTitle: Organizational tailoring of the CMM questionnaire for internal process improvement [software development management]
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Some organizations are attempting to reduce the time and cost required by formal process improvement models by tailoring those models to specific needs. This paper describes a tailored version of the Software Engineering Institute's (SEI) capability maturity model (CMM) questionnaire which was developed by a large US-based Fortune 500 company for low-cost internal process improvement purposes.

articleTitle: Technology and know-how transfer as part of a market establishing process: decision-making issues in culturally different markets
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Technology transfer to developing markets is part of the market establishing process. However, culturally-based differences in decision-making between the countries involved in the transfer process can delay business ventures or make them impossible. By understanding the different decision-making issues, the success rate can be increased and disappointments prevented.

articleTitle: Engineering and technology management for a more sustainable development
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. Sustainable development is a rather new concept that emerged because of the increasing awareness that the environment is endangered by the intensification of human technological activities producing a rapid decrease of nonrenewable resources, among which are fossil fuels, and a rapid increase of soil, water and air pollution rates. This paper presents two requirements that should be fulfilled in order that engineering and technology contribute more efficiently to the major issue of sustainable development: (i) the adaptation of engineering curricula of most engineering schools in order to take into account the new issues of a sustainable development; and (ii) the reactivation of world-wide public, democratically elected organizations whose specific task would be to define and to rule-through economic and moral incentives-the engineering and technology R&D priorities according to "sustainability" values based on intra- and inter-generational equity and solidarity.

articleTitle: The application of concurrent engineering in small to medium enterprises
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary for only given. Concurrent engineering has been developed and practiced by large multi-national companies working in consumer oriented industries. As a result, the implementation methods, tools and techniques have been geared towards these industries. Some of these methods, tools and techniques, cannot be easily applied in small to medium sized companies in traditional industries. During the world recession of the early 1990s, it became clear to the 600 Group management that the company must adopt a market led approach and that it must have the ability to react quickly to the market needs. Concurrent engineering was recognized as the philosophy that would enable rapid new product introduction. Three issues were fundamental to 600 Lathes Concurrent Engineering practice, project initiation, involving all functional disciplines, teamwork, and risk management. It was necessary to adapt the general principles to use them in a medium sized manufacturing company. None of the concurrent engineering techniques were used formally. However, the underlying philosophies were informally used to good effect. Teamwork made the most significant contribution. Inspite of not formally using some of the recognised tools and techniques of concurrent engineering, for example, quality function deployment (QFD) and failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), the application of the generic principles resulted in significant benefits. The use of parallel work philosophy in a team environment reduced the product introduction lead-time by 30% and the cost by a third.

articleTitle: Social and economic challenges affecting management in 2005
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. An evolution from the industrial age to the service age appears to be the next major driver affecting the world economy. The service age will be dominated by professional service providers at every level of society, from the household domestics and "McDonald's" jobs to the highly skilled individual contributors. The focus of 'employment', from a management perspective, is changing from reuse of the current workforce (lifetime job security) to that acquisition of best value, experience, resilience and abilities. The authors describe how this shift is driving the workforce to change its concept of, and requirements for, employment.

articleTitle: Autopoiesis and strategic management in emerging economies
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given. For businesses in developing countries, the 1990s is a period of incipient changes. The main change has come about when economies like that of India were thrown open to global competition under the process of liberalization or globalization. Strategic rethinking to respond to the market imperatives has assumed urgent priority. The conventional strategic management methodology, based on a 'vision-based' model, is being replaced by autopoietic models, where causality no longer holds good. This is a process that undergoes changes due to fluctuations almost in a random fashion, but order gets developed through self-organization. Business organizations exhibit characteristics of autonomy. One feature of autonomy in institutions/firms is, when impacted by the environment, they respond in such a way as to preserve their own identity. An important attribute of autopoietic models is that they are complex, nonlinear and hence their future evolution is unpredictable. Strategic thinking and management has to deal with these new models for effective outcomes. Business systems, under conditions of fluctuations due to variations in the business environment, assume a different order depending on the environment. By tracking these fluctuations, learning and self-learning has to take place in the firm to initiate innovations in response to these fluctuations. The paper elaborates on this type of model and recommends steps to base management strategy for effective implementation.

articleTitle: Managing the systems engineering process in a changing environment
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Rarely do requirements remain static during the systems engineering process. Customer needs change as additional information becomes known. Organizations that are essential to the success of the product are brought into the process after the design or development of the product is underway. Technology enhancements in the components utilized in the platform create new capabilities which result in changes in the requirements. This paper addresses the process of managing change within the systems engineering process. It includes a review of the tools and procedures which facilitate the process of managing changing requirements while keeping the development of the product on target.

articleTitle: Managing ergonomics and technology in a large corporation
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. The effective application of computer technology involves more than just the computing hardware and software. It also involves the human interface to that equipment. This becomes increasingly important as more functions require computer use and computers are used for longer periods of time. Management and employees both need to be aware of ergonomic factors in computer use. Also, ergonomic computer use issues can extend beyond the work place to home use of computers. Ergonomic considerations are important to management in avoiding employee pain and injury and in establishing a productive work place.

articleTitle: Manufacturing to demand: initial explorations in linking product with market modelling
publicationTitle: Innovation in Technology Management. The Key to Global Leadership. PICMET '97
abstract: Summary form only given as follows. Enterprise integration, which requires the interconnection of business processes, is just one means of improving the competitiveness of an organization. The research reported here discusses an approach that offers the potential to link the seemingly disparate areas of manufacturing, marketing and distribution. Many organizations are becoming market rather than production driven and we believe that links between the market and production can make a major contribution to their agility. Product data engineering research in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Leeds was established some 10 years ago and is currently directed towards understanding the role of product and manufacturing models and structures in business processes. Researchers in the School of Geography at Leeds have developed a set of mathematical models that allow the richness and complexity of today's consumer markets to be understood and predicted. These models have been successfully applied to the automotive industry and are now being used by a major automotive company to develop a distribution strategy for the year 2000 both in Europe and North America. This research couples these two strands of research by making use of mathematical models of consumer markets together with product data engineering work on the representation of product specifications. A product specification captures the functional characteristics that a product must satisfy. This paper reports an early exploration which was undertaken using the automotive industry as a case study.
